title: Elicited Adaptation: Auditable Localized Fairness via Pairwise Queries
claim: The exact cost curve is piecewise linear with a plateau, so the initial slope alone misses the budget needed at larger scales.
layout: 1 panel, line plot, dashed bound versus solid exact curve, plateau in middle
description: A single wide line plot with a light grid and a black frame. The x-axis is budget a, with ticks at 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3. The y-axis is cost, from 0 to about 0.3. A thick solid black line, labeled 'Exact cost curve', rises with slope 2 from the origin to (0.05, 0.1). It then stays flat until a = 0.1, rises again with a gentler slope to (0.3, 0.3), and stays flat after that. A thin gray dashed line, labeled 'Bound min{2a, .3}', rises steeply to 0.3 at a = 0.15 and then runs flat. The legend sits in the upper left and partly overlaps the dashed line. The eye goes first to the thick black curve with its flat shelf in the middle. The dashed bound above it shows the gap between the bound and the exact curve.
caption: Exact cost curve for a six-profile, one-target instance with two disconnected components: a single edge with source budget .8 and target budget .2, and a three-edge source path of budget .2 per edge whose target contains the first and last edges with budget .1. Their costs are min{𝑎, .3} and min{2𝑎, .1}, respectively; the overall cost is their maximum. The resulting curve resumes increasing after a plateau. Thus 𝐾= 2 determines the initial slope, while the full curve determines the budget at larger scales. The appendix verifies the formula directly.
abstract: How much must a predictor's scores change when a community's elicited fairness standard changes? Similarity and tolerance judgments define protected comparisons and acceptable score gaps. We study minimum uniform score movement on a fixed pool of $n$ profiles. For scores satisfying a source standard, we characterize the exact cost of retaining that standard during adaptation: runs of consecutive target constraints along shortest paths determine the optimal amplification factor. Its sharp worst case is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, and a full cost curve describes finite target-only repair budgets. Committing before the target is known can cost $n-1$ times the worst repair after revelation, even within one fixed convex ball of two-dimensional Mahalanobis metrics. Positive edge-budget floors cap both factors; bounded geometry also limits the commitment cost. At two interior targets of the construction attaining the $n-1$ bound, similarity queries alone yield a feasible $2$-approximate repair for tolerance $\eps\le1/[2(n-1)]$, reducing movement relative to common repair by a factor linear in $n$. Feasible $(1+Î±)$-optimal repair on this family has worst-case tolerance-query complexity $Î(Î±^{-2}n^2\log(1/Î´))$ under a fixed-slope logistic model. The analysis separates the information needed for a substantial adaptation benefit from the precision needed for nearly optimal movement. Elicitation studies and training comparisons examine tolerance choice and the relation between numerical compliance and predictive utility.
